title: Before You Were Mine

cards.story: A grown-up daughter speaks to her mother. Using old photos and her mum’s stories, she imagines her mother as a fun-loving teenager in Glasgow, ten years before the daughter was born. Then she remembers her own childhood with her.
cards.message: Before she was a mum, your mother was a young woman with her own life, freedom and fun. Having a child changed that. The daughter loves her, admires her, and is a little jealous of the girl she can never meet.
cards.why: Duffy calls it “essentially a kind of love poem addressed to my mother” and says it is “entirely autobiographical”. The images “come from old photographs of my mother.” Sheer Poetry, via University of Glasgow Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source

title_note.heading: The title
title_note.text: “Mine” is a word lovers use, and Duffy calls this “a kind of love poem” to her mother. Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source But here it is a child claiming a parent, as if saying that her mother belongs to her. The title phrase comes back in line 9 and again as the very last words of the poem, so the poem keeps returning to the time before the daughter owned her. The University of Glasgow calls this “a cyclical structure”. the ideas about lovers and ownership are our reading
title_note.src: Duffy’s words as quoted in a University of Glasgow guide; University of Glasgow teaching resource; AQA anthology

synopsis.setup: The speaker is a grown-up daughter talking straight to her mother (“you”). She is not there in the scenes she describes: they happened before she was born. Most of it is in the present tense, so the past feels as if it is happening now.

steps.text: She places herself <q>“ten years away”</q> from her mother, who is laughing on a street corner with her friends (<q>“your pals”</q>), named as Maggie McGeeney and Jean Duff.

The three girls double up with laughter and <q>“shriek at the pavement.”</q> The mother’s polka-dot dress blows round her legs, and the daughter adds one word: <q>“Marilyn.”</q> (the film star Marilyn Monroe).
<q>“I’m not here yet.”</q> At the dance hall, the young woman is not thinking about a baby at all. She is dreaming of exciting, film-like futures: <q>“the fizzy, movie tomorrows”</q>.

The daughter is sure her mother danced well. Back home, the mother’s own mum (“your Ma”) waits at the entrance to the flats (the close) to give her a beating (a hiding) for being late. The girl thinks the fun was “worth it.”

Now the daughter’s birth arrives: her <q>“loud, possessive yell”</q>. She asks if the ten years before it were the best ones, <q>“eh?”</q> She remembers playing with her mother’s old red high heels, now <q>“relics”</q>.

In the present, she pictures the young version of her mother (<q>“your ghost”</q>) hurrying across George Square in Glasgow. She sees her under a tree with lights and teases her about love bites: <q>“sweetheart?”</q>

A childhood memory: walking home from church (<q>“Mass”</q>), her mother teaches her dance steps (<q>“Cha cha cha!”</q>). Even then, the child wanted the bold, flirty girl her mother used to be. That girl lives on, dancing and laughing, <q>“before you were mine.”</q>

synopsis.turn: The turning point (line 11): stanza 3 jumps forward to the daughter’s birth, her “loud, possessive yell”. Stanzas 1–2 are the mother’s life without her; stanzas 3–4 mix the daughter’s own memories with that lost past.
synopsis.ending: The last line returns to the title phrase. The daughter cannot have the young woman, but in her imagination that girl lasts for ever: <q>“you sparkle and waltz and laugh”</q>. The ending is joyful and a little sad at the same time.
synopsis.tone: Warm, chatty and teasing (<q>“eh?”</q>, <q>“sweetheart?”</q>), full of glamour and fun. AQA’s 2023 mark scheme points to “the sense of joy and celebration” in the poem. Underneath there is longing, and some envy, for the girl the daughter never knew.

poem_intro: Highlighted words are the ones worth quoting in the exam.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>I’m ten years away from the corner you laugh on</mark> … <mark>shriek at the pavement.</mark> … <mark>Marilyn.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: The daughter measures the gap between them in time: ten years before her birth. Her mother is a teenager on a Glasgow street corner, laughing with friends. The real names (Maggie McGeeney and Jean Duff) make it feel true. The girls are loud and free. Then a one-word sentence: Marilyn. Duffy says one old photo “reminded me of the famous image of Marilyn Monroe where her dress is blowing up around her knees”. Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source

poem_blocks.text: <mark>I’m not here yet.</mark> … <mark>the fizzy, movie tomorrows</mark> … <mark>You reckon it’s worth it.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: A short, blunt sentence: the daughter does not exist yet, and her mother is not thinking about her. At the dance hall (“the ballroom with the thousand eyes”, which the University of Glasgow suggests “may refer to a mirrorball”) the girl dreams of a future like a film. Duffy says her mother told “tales about the weekend search in the ballrooms of Glasgow for “Mr Right”!” Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source At home, her strict mother waits at the close (a Scottish word for the passage or shared stairway into a block of flats) with a beating. The girl thinks the fun is worth the trouble: she is rebellious and independent.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>my loud, possessive yell</mark> … <mark>high-heeled red shoes, relics,</mark> … <mark>your ghost clatters toward me</mark>
poem_blocks.note: Now the baby is born. Her first cry is “possessive”: from the start she claims her mother. She wonders if the decade before was “the best one, eh?”, which sounds jokey but also guilty. As a small child she put her hands in her mother’s old red high heels. Calling them relics (precious objects from the past, like a saint’s belongings) shows that the glamorous girl is gone. The ghost is that young self, not a dead mother: the daughter imagines her clattering over George Square in her heels, “clear as scent”, under a lit-up tree.

poem_blocks.text: <mark>Cha cha cha!</mark> … <mark>stamping stars from the wrong pavement.</mark> … <mark>you sparkle and waltz and laugh before you were mine.</mark>
poem_blocks.note: A real childhood memory: mother and daughter dance home from Mass (Catholic church). Duffy says this part is set in England, and that metal studs on their shoes “would make sparks on the pavement as we stamped out the steps.” Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source So the stars are real sparks. Even then the child wanted the “bold girl” in Portobello, “somewhere / in Scotland”. (There is a seaside Portobello near Edinburgh; that the poem means it is our reading.) The final line keeps that girl moving for ever in a list of happy verbs, then ends on the title.

quotes.q: I'm ten years away from the corner you laugh on
quotes.means: she pictures her mother ten years before her own birth.
quotes.why: it measures distance in time, not miles. The mother is in the present tense (“laugh”), so the past feels alive, while the daughter can only watch from outside.

quotes.q: Your polka-dot dress blows round your legs. Marilyn.
quotes.means: her mother looked like the film star Marilyn Monroe.
quotes.tech: a one-word sentence and an allusion (a reference to something famous). It turns an ordinary street into a film set, and the mother into a glamorous star.

quotes.why: a short, blunt sentence. It reminds us that the mother’s freedom belongs to the time before the child, and hints at the change the child will bring.

quotes.means: the baby’s first cry, claiming her mother.
quotes.tech: the adjective “possessive” links to “mine” in the title. AQA’s 2023 mark scheme suggests “ideas about possession/ownership in the parent/child relationship”.

quotes.means: her mother’s old party shoes, kept but no longer worn.
quotes.why: “relics” are holy objects from the past. The shoes stand for the glamorous girl, who now exists only as a memory. Red suggests passion and fun.

quotes.q: your ghost clatters toward me over George Square
quotes.means: she imagines her mother’s young self rushing across Glasgow’s main square.
quotes.why: the “ghost” is the young woman who has gone, not a dead mother. AQA warns some students wrongly think “the speaker’s mother has died”. “clatters” lets us hear her heels.

quotes.q: you sparkle and waltz and laugh before you were mine.
quotes.means: in the daughter’s imagination, the young girl dances and laughs for ever.
quotes.tech: a list of verbs joined by “and” (polysyndeton) keeps her moving. The poem ends by repeating the title, so it circles back to the past.

form.heading: The form: four neat stanzas, a chatty voice, and time that won’t stay still
explain: The poem has four stanzas of five lines each (quintains). The University of Glasgow says this “gives the poem a clear and controlled shape”. University of Glasgow; our count

There is no regular rhyme or rhythm: it is close to free verse. The same source says this “gives the poem a natural and conversational tone, like someone remembering and reflecting.” University of Glasgow; our count one source

It is written in the second person: the speaker talks to “you”, her mother. AQA’s 2017 mark scheme names the “second person in ‘Before You Were Mine’” as a method worth writing about. AQA mark scheme 2017
this_poem: Three time zones: the poem “shifts between past and present, from the time before the speaker was born, her own childhood, and the present day.” University of Glasgow Stanzas 1–2 are the mother’s youth; stanza 3 brings in the daughter’s birth and childhood; “and now” jumps to the present; stanza 4 goes back to childhood and then to the youth again.
Present tense for the past: “you laugh”, “your Ma stands”. The mother’s youth is told as if it is happening now, so the daughter seems to be watching a film of it. our reading
A circle: the title words appear in line 9 and as the final words. The poem cannot move forward to the present; it keeps going back to the girl “before”. our reading

Talking voice: questions and slang (“eh?”, “sweetheart?”, “You reckon”) make it sound like a daughter teasing her mum. The neat stanzas hold this chat in a careful shape, like photos in an album. our reading
form.say: A sentence you could use: Duffy speaks straight to her mother as “you” and uses the present tense for a past she never saw, so the young woman feels alive; but by ending on the title, “before you were mine”, the poem circles back to a time the daughter can imagine but never share.

methods.title: Direct address and shifting time
methods.text: Everything is spoken to <q>“you”</q>. The poem moves between before the daughter’s birth, her childhood and the present, marked by phrases like <q>“I’m not here yet.”</q>, <q>“I remember”</q> and <q>“and now”</q>. This shows a child slowly seeing her parent as a person with her own past.
methods.def: writing to “you”, as if speaking straight to someone.

methods.title: Hollywood glamour
methods.text: “Marilyn.”, “movie tomorrows”, “sparkle”, “That glamorous love lasts”. The young mother is shown as a film star. Duffy says her mother “glamourised her young self” in the stories she told, so the mother “is perceived almost as a movie star”. Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source
methods.def: a reference to a famous person, story or thing that the reader is expected to know.

methods.title: Possessive words
methods.text: The title’s “mine”, the baby’s “possessive yell”, and “I wanted the bold girl”. The child claims the mother, yet also wants the free girl that motherhood ended. Duffy says the poem is about “a child’s almost possessive love for her mother”. Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source
methods.def: a word that shows ownership, such as “my”, “mine”, “your”.

methods.title: A chatty, local voice
methods.text: Everyday spoken words fill the poem: “pals”, “your Ma”, “a hiding”, “You reckon”, “eh?”. “the close” is a Scottish word for a narrow lane or shared stairwell, and a real Glasgow place appears: George Square. They make it feel like a true family story. Duffy was born in Glasgow. Britannica; University of Glasgow
methods.def: informal, everyday speech, including slang and local words.

warn: Examiners warn: “A small minority of students misunderstand ‘Before You Were Mine’ and think that the speaker’s mother has died, which is a shame as it means they can miss the point of the poem.” The “ghost” is her mother’s young self. AQA praised answers that read the poem as “the speaker’s desire to understand the woman their mother was before she was a mother, with perhaps an undertone of envy / longing”. (AQA examiners’ report, June 2023)

items.text: Born in Glasgow in 1955 to parents of Irish Catholic descent. The University of Glasgow says she was “the eldest of five children in a Roman Catholic family”, born in the Gorbals, a working-class area.
items.care: the Gorbals and “eldest of five”: one source (University of Glasgow)

items.text: Her family moved to Stafford, England, when she was six. So the Glasgow of the poem is her mother’s world and her own earliest years.
items.care: the second sentence is our reading

items.text: From 2009 to 2019 she was the first woman Poet Laureate. Simon Armitage, who wrote Mother, any distance, took over from her.
She also wrote War Photographer (Power and conflict). Both poems are about looking at photographs and the stories behind them.
“BEFORE YOU WERE MINE is essentially a kind of love poem addressed to my mother. It is entirely autobiographical.”

items.text: Marilyn Monroe was “a major sex symbol” of the 1950s. In The Seven Year Itch (1955) her white dress billows up over a subway grate. That film came out in Duffy’s birth year, ten years after the scene, so the comparison is the grown-up daughter’s, looking back.
items.care: the last sentence is our reading

items.text: Dance halls were where young men and women met; the University of Glasgow says they offered “self-expression and an escape from home life.” Duffy says her mother searched “the ballrooms of Glasgow for “Mr Right””.

items.text: George Square is “in the heart of Glasgow”, its main open space. The poem’s Portobello is “somewhere in Scotland”. There is a seaside Portobello “3 miles (5 km) east of the centre of Edinburgh”. Real places make the mother’s youth feel solid.
items.care: one source each; that the poem means Edinburgh’s Portobello is our reading

cards.title: What AQA says about this poem

items.text: June 2023 printed it with the question: “Compare how poets present relationships between parents and children”.
The 2023 mark scheme suggests “ideas about possession/ownership in the parent/child relationship” and “how parenthood impacts upon sense of self/individual identity”.
It also points to “the sense of joy and celebration in ‘Before You Were Mine’”, compared with the “more ambiguous tone of ‘Follower’ or ‘Mother, Any Distance’”.
In 2023, Follower and Mother, any distance “were by far the most popular choices of second poem”, with “lots of choices of ‘Eden Rock’, ‘Walking Away’ and ‘Climbing My Grandfather’”.

context.ao3: Putting it into an answer (AO3): Duffy built the poem from old photographs of her mother and calls it “a kind of love poem”. She says it is about “the freedom a woman loses when she has a child”. Duffy’s words, quoted by the University of Glasgow; one source So the daughter’s “possessive yell” is loving but also the end of the mother’s carefree youth, which is why the poem mixes celebration with a quiet sense of envy and longing.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2023 mark scheme (“feelings towards a parent and how these might change, eg ‘Follower’ or ‘Mother, Any Distance’”); specimen mark scheme (“the passage of time and its impact on attitudes in ‘Mother, Any Distance’ or ‘Before You Were Mine’”); 2023 report: the most popular second poem
similar: Both speak straight to a mother as “you”: <q>“You come to help me measure”</q> and <q>“the corner you laugh on”</q>. Both are by Poets Laureate (Duffy, then Armitage).
Both are about the distance between mother and child, and both measure it: <q>“Mother, any distance”</q> in space, <q>“ten years away”</q> in time.
Both show that loving someone means holding on. Duffy’s baby claims her mother with a <q>“possessive yell”</q>; Armitage’s mother grips the tape with <q>“your fingertips still pinch”</q>.
different: Who holds on: in Duffy, the child is possessive and wants the mother. In Armitage, the mother clings on while the son pulls away.
Direction in time: Duffy looks back to her mother’s freedom before motherhood: “before I was born.” Armitage looks forward to the son’s own freedom: “an endless sky”.
Tone: AQA’s 2023 mark scheme contrasts “the sense of joy and celebration” in Duffy with the “more ambiguous tone” of Mother, any distance, which ends on a risk: “to fall or fly.”
Form: Duffy’s four even five-line stanzas look back calmly; Armitage’s last stanza stretches to seven lines, like the tape. our reading

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2023 mark scheme (Follower suggested for this question); specimen mark scheme (“speaker in ‘Follower’ and speaker in … ‘Before You Were Mine’”); 2025 mark scheme (“admiration for an adult family figure, such as ‘Before You Were Mine’”)
similar: Both children admire a parent’s skill. Heaney’s father is <q>“An expert.”</q> at ploughing; Duffy is sure of her mother’s dancing: <q>“I knew you would dance”</q>.
Both children want to copy the parent, using the same words: <q>“I wanted to grow up and plough,”</q> and <q>“I wanted the bold girl”</q>. Both learn by following: <q>“You’d teach me the steps”</q>.
Both are adults remembering childhood, and AQA’s 2025 mark scheme names “use of memory/incidents as symbolic of ideas” in Duffy’s poem.
different: Parent: Heaney admires his father’s hard work on the farm; Duffy admires her mother’s fun and glamour before she had a child.
Ending: Follower reverses the roles: now “It is my father who keeps stumbling”. Duffy does not move to the present; she ends back in the past, “before you were mine.”
Tone: AQA contrasts Duffy’s “joy and celebration” with the “more ambiguous tone of ‘Follower’”, where the father becomes a burden.
Form: Follower uses six rhymed four-line stanzas; Duffy uses four unrhymed five-line stanzas in a chatty voice.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2023 mark scheme (Eden Rock suggested for this question); Nov 2020 mark scheme (“use of memory to present ideas, eg ‘Eden Rock’ or ‘Before You Were Mine’”); 2025 mark scheme (“comparative presentation of parents”)
similar: Both picture a parent when young, as if in an old photo, even down to the dress: <q>“My mother, twenty-three, in a sprigged dress”</q> and <q>“Your polka-dot dress”</q>.
Both blur time: the parents appear young again, in vivid detail, though the speaker is now grown up.
Both give real, everyday details (a Thermos, an H.P. Sauce bottle; <q>“your Ma stands at the close”</q>) to make the memory feel solid.
different: Who is reaching whom: Causley’s parents call the speaker to join them: “They beckon to me from the other bank.” Duffy can never join her mother’s youth: “I’m not here yet.”

Life and death: Eden Rock is often read as the speaker approaching his own death and meeting his dead parents. In Duffy the mother is alive; the “ghost” is her young self. our reading of Eden Rock; AQA warns against reading Duffy’s mother as dead
Mood: Causley’s scene is calm and still, ending in surprise: “I had not thought that it would be like this.” Duffy’s is noisy and lively, full of shrieks, dancing and “Cha cha cha!”

exam_box.question: A likely question: Compare how poets present relationships between parents and children in ‘Before You Were Mine’ and in one other poem from ‘Love and relationships’. (AQA, June 2023)
exam_box.thesis: Both Duffy and Armitage show that a child’s love for a parent includes a wish to possess, but in Duffy it is the daughter who longs for the free girl her mother was, while in Armitage it is the mother who cannot let her son go.
exam_box.para: Both poets present the parent–child bond as a kind of ownership. Duffy’s title claims the mother as <q>“mine”</q>, and the baby’s first sound is a <q>“possessive yell”</q>, suggesting the child’s arrival takes over her mother’s life. Yet the daughter envies the girl she replaced: <q>“I wanted the bold girl”</q>. Armitage reverses who holds on. The son climbs away while his mother’s <q>“fingertips still pinch”</q> the tape, refusing to let go. Their views of time also differ. Duffy looks back, so the mother’s freedom is fixed in the past where <q>“you sparkle and waltz and laugh”</q>. Armitage looks forward to <q>“an endless sky”</q>. Together they suggest that parenthood costs freedom: Duffy’s mother lost hers, and Armitage’s son must win his.
why: Thesis answers the question in one sentence and names the key difference (who holds on)
Uses AQA’s own idea of “possession/ownership” with short quotations from both poems, analysing single words (“mine”, “possessive”, “still”)
Compares how each poem handles time (looking back vs looking forward) and ends with a judgement linked to parents and children
